title: Do You Want Us to Pull Them Up?
subtitle: An enemy in the dark, a loyal offer at dawn, and the No that keeps the field alive
teaser: The weeds went in at night; the offer to fix them came at dawn and sounded like loyalty. Jesus hangs the whole parable on the refusal — and a psalm had answered the servants a thousand years before they asked: do not fret, be still — the grass is already withering.
theme: Building day: the whole parable at full weight — night sabotage, the servants' offer, the Master's No, and the psalmist's stillness for the fretful
framework: Matthew 13:30 - Let both grow together until the harvest

modules.passage: 'An enemy did this,' he replied. So the servants asked him, 'Do you want us to go and pull them up?' 'No,' he said, 'if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest.'
emphasis: Do you want us to go and pull them up?
Let both grow together until the harvest
modules.scriptureContext: Two minutes inside the exchange the whole story exists to set up: a loyal offer, and the refusal that saves the field from its friends.

modules.definition: let, permit, leave — the imperative of aphiēmi, Matthew's verb for FORGIVE
modules.usage: "Let both grow together" — the command is built on the same Greek verb the Lord's Prayer uses for forgive: aphes hēmin, forgive us our debts. When the Master refuses the pulling, He is conjugating pardon into farm policy — and whoever you had privately given up on is standing inside that grammar this morning.

modules.prompt: A name crossed your mind during that exchange. When you think of that person, whose voice do you hear in your own — the servants offering to pull, or the Master saying let?

modules.heading: A Two-Minute Prayer
modules.prayerText: Master of the field, You answered sabotage with three calm words and met loyalty's worst idea with a No. I meet far less with far more panic. Before I pull at anyone today — especially the one whose name just surfaced — put Your verb in my mouth: let. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: That was a whole reading. Below: the night the weeds went in, the two reasons the Master spoke and the one He saved, the psalm that had already answered the servants — and the slave-ship captain no honest inspection would have spared.

modules.passage: Jesus put before them another parable: "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away. When the wheat sprouted and bore grain, then the weeds also appeared. The owner's servants came to him and said, 'Sir, didn't you sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?' 'An enemy did this,' he replied. So the servants asked him, 'Do you want us to go and pull them up?' 'No,' he said, 'if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest. At that time I will tell the harvesters: First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn.'"
modules.greekOriginal: ἄφετε συναυξάνεσθαι ἀμφότερα ἕως τοῦ θερισμοῦ
modules.transliteration: aphete synauxanesthai amphotera heōs tou therismou — "let both grow together until the harvest"
emphasis: But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away.
Let both grow together until the harvest
modules.scriptureContext: The parable entire, in one breath — good sowing, night sabotage, delayed discovery, loyal offer, and the No this week turns on.

modules.definition: to grow together — to increase side by side
modules.usage: This word appears exactly once in the New Testament: here. The kingdom's crop, in Jesus' telling, does not mature in a greenhouse. It grows up entangled — root to root with what opposes it — and reaches harvest anyway. Purity of environment is not a condition of the wheat's survival.
modules.usageNote: Pair it with the command that governs it: ἄφετε (aphete), the imperative of ἀφίημι (aphiēmi, G863) — release, permit, leave, and, throughout Matthew, FORGIVE: ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν, 'forgive us our debts' (6:12). Jesus could have chosen a colorless word for 'allow.' He chose the one His hearers already prayed.

relatedWords.meaning: "forgive us" — the same verb, four chapters earlier, on every disciple's lips

modules.heading: The Night Before the Question
modules.content:
Yesterday closed on a generous hand and a lengthening shadow: seed thrown wide over every kind of ground, and a hint that the sower is not the only one who visits fields. Today Jesus tells the next parable, and the shadow gets a name. The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field — so far, familiar. Then the sentence that turns farming into a thriller: but while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away.

Sit with the details Jesus chose. The sabotage takes one visit, under cover of the field's most innocent hour — everyone asleep, nobody derelict, just night doing what night does. And the crime stays invisible for months. Only when the wheat sprouted and bore grain, the parable says, did the weeds also appear. Read that again: the sabotage surfaces only when the good crop starts producing. The first evidence anyone sees of the enemy's work is grain. Fruitfulness is what exposes the counterfeit growing beside it.

The servants respond the way good servants should. They go to the owner, not the rumor mill. They ask about the seed before assuming the worst about the sower: Sir, didn't you sow good seed in your field? They receive his three-word diagnosis — an enemy did this — without argument. And then they volunteer for the obvious mission: Do you want us to go and pull them up? Loyal, brave, aimed squarely at the enemy's work. Nothing in their offer deserves rebuke, and none arrives. What arrives is a No.

You have made their offer. Perhaps not against an enemy — the offers we make most fluently are aimed nearer home, at the one who told you, kindly enough, that belief is behind them and the topic is closed. Somewhere along the way, without ceremony, you may have concluded on their behalf that the growing was over. That conclusion is the servants' offer, whispered — and the No is coming for it too.

But before the reasons, look back once at the dark, because the picture below is the whole provocation: a figure moving through a sleeping field, scattering ruin, already leaving. He comes, he sows, he slips away — and the story never shows him again.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A cloaked figure slipping away through a moonlit field at night, a trail of scattered seed behind him
modules.inlineImageCaption: While everyone slept, the enemy came, sowed weeds among the wheat, and slipped away — and the parable never shows him again.

modules.content: The sabotage took one night. The rescue is what would have ruined the field.

modules.heading: Why the No Holds
modules.content:
The Master gives one reason aloud; the field itself supplies a second; the third He saves. Take them in order.

The spoken reason is mechanical: if you pull the weeds now, you might uproot the wheat with them. Wheat and darnel sown into the same soil do not keep polite distances underground. By the time either shows above the surface, their roots have braided, and a fist closing around one stalk closes around its neighbors. Lives braid the same way, only tighter: marriages, congregations, friendships, shared histories. There is no such thing as extracting one human being cleanly. Church history keeps the receipts — every movement that promised surgical purity has pulled up wheat by the armful, and some of it never went back in the ground.

The unspoken reason is standing in the furrows: nobody present can perform the inspection. Darnel — bearded darnel, Lolium temulentum, the zizania of verse 25 — is wheat's double for most of its life. Easton's Bible Dictionary puts it flatly: "It bears the closest resemblance to wheat till the ear appears, and only then the difference is discovered." Until heads form, the knowledge the servants would need does not exist — not hidden from them; not yet in the world. And heads form at harvest. Whatever is true of plants is doubly true of persons: the evidence that would justify a sentence over anybody's life has not finished happening.

The third reason Jesus keeps in reserve. The disciples will get it from His own mouth tomorrow, symbol by symbol, when He decodes the story indoors — and the deepest logic of the delay will come with it. But the church's earliest readers heard that logic under the surface of the No centuries ago — and their answer is waiting a little further down this page.

modules.heading: Ancient Truth, Modern Life
modules.ancientTruth: The servants' itch is older than the servants. A thousand years earlier, David watched evil flourish in the field of the world and wrote down both the urge and its cure: "Do not fret over those who do evil… For they wither quickly like grass and wilt like tender plants" (Psalm 37:1-2). The psalm's remedy points the opposite direction entirely: "Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him" (37:7). Israel had been singing the answer for centuries before Jesus narrated the question.
modules.modernApplication: Fretting has upgraded its equipment: the 2 a.m. replay of what they said, the feed refreshed to keep the outrage warm, the running indictment rehearsed in the shower. Psalm 37 calls all of it by one name and hands over the same prescription it has always carried: stillness, patience, and a longer view of grass.
modules.connectionPoint: The psalm and the parable share their agronomy. "They wither quickly like grass" is God's own forecast for evil — darnel has no future beyond the field, and the fretful eye keeps forgetting it. The psalm asks for stillness precisely because the weeds matter: Someone with better eyes has the matter in hand, and the grass was never going to outlast the grain.
modules.newTestamentEcho: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." — Matthew 6:12 (BSB). Aphete, the 'let' of 'let both grow,' and aphes, the 'forgive' of the Lord's Prayer, are one Greek verb: what David called being still before the LORD, Jesus conjugates as pardon.

modules.heading: The Reason Under the Reasons
modules.content:
Now for the reason Jesus is saving for tomorrow's interpretation. The church of the martyr centuries heard it early — readers with every earthly excuse to want a sickle, listening hard under the Master's No.

John Chrysostom, preaching through Matthew in the fourth century, put it plainly: "Either He means this, If you are to take up arms, and to kill the heretics, many of the saints also must needs be overthrown with them; or that of the very tares it is likely that many may change and become wheat. If therefore ye root them up beforehand, you injure that which is to become wheat, slaying some, in whom there is yet room for change and improvement." Read that second clause again. In a real field, darnel is darnel until it dies. In THIS field, the tares can change kind. Chrysostom pressed the point to its edge — and kept both edges: "So long as they stand by the wheat, we must spare them, for it is possible for them even to become wheat; but when they have departed, having profited nothing, then of necessity the inexorable punishment will overtake them." The door stands open, and the door closes: mercy with a deadline is still mercy — and still a deadline.

Augustine, a generation later, said it with a preacher's economy: "I say this to the evil, who yet are Christians; I say this to the tares. For they are in the field; and it may so be, that they who to-day are tares, may to-morrow be wheat." And when a rigorist movement in North Africa demanded a purified church NOW — a field with the mixture already removed — Augustine answered from this same image: the Lord's threshing-floor "must needs contain, up to the time of the final winnowing, both grain which is to be stored in the garner, and chaff that is to be burned up with fire."

Here, then, is the reason under the reasons. The Master's No is ambition, not resignation. Every season the field stays mixed is a season the darnel is being given to defect. The patience that scandalizes the servants is aimed precisely at the stalks they wanted to burn — which means the uprooting they offered would not merely have cost some wheat. It would have foreclosed every future conversion in the field. Say it in church-history terms: a sickle taken to the field in the late 1740s harvests a young slave-trading sailor named John Newton as darnel, and no one ever sings Amazing Grace.

Be honest about the record, too: the church has not always listened to its own fathers here. The same centuries that copied out Chrysostom's homily also built inquisitions; the parable's No has been read aloud by people sharpening sickles. That record argues not for softening the text but for keeping it sharp: every generation's servants make the same reasonable offer, and the Master's answer has not changed.

modules.inlineImageAlt: An underground cross-section showing two plants whose roots are completely intertwined, a warm glow at the center
modules.inlineImageCaption: Below the surface the roots are already tangled — uprooting the one would tear out the other.

modules.heading: The Darnel That Wrote the Hymn
modules.content:
By any field inspection conducted in the 1740s, John Newton was darnel — and not ambiguously. A press-ganged sailor turned slave-trader, he had even been, in his own words, "in effect, though without the name, a Captive and a Slave myself" on the African coast. If ever a stalk deserved pulling, it was this one.

Then came the storm. "The 10th (that is, in the present style, the 21st) of March, is a day much to be remembered by me," he wrote, "and I have never suffered it to pass wholly unnoticed since the year 1748. On that day the Lord sent from on high, and delivered me out of deep waters." He had pumped the flooding ship from three in the morning until noon and steered her until midnight, praying for the first time in years. But here the story refuses to become the clean conversion tale we want — and its honesty is the point. The newly praying Newton went back to the trade. He sailed from Liverpool in 1750 as commander of a slave ship and made three voyages as captain, holding worship on deck "twice every Lord's day, officiating myself," while the hold beneath him carried its cargo. "I never had a scruple upon this head at the time," he confessed later, "nor was such a thought once suggested to me, by any friend." Only a sudden fit in 1754, the day before a fourth voyage, took him off the ships — not conviction; illness.

The wheat in him grew slowly — by decades, not seasons — entangled with the darnel of his age and his own seared conscience. In time came ordination, the little parish of Olney, and the hymn the whole world knows. And forty years after the storm, the old pastor finally published his confession against the trade: "a public confession, which, however sincere, comes too late to prevent, or repair, the misery and mischief to which I have, formerly, been accessary… I was, once, an active instrument, in a business at which my heart now shudders." He lived just long enough to see Britain abolish that trade in 1807.

Inspect Newton at any single point — the trader on the coast, the praying captain above the hold, the man a sudden fit rather than conviction finally took off the ships — and every reading returns the same result, decade after decade of it. Anyone who loved him had a lifetime of evidence for despair, and all of it was wrong, because the God of this field was not finished. What no single glance could see, the whole growing season proved: wheat had been coming up in that man the entire time.
modules.connectionToTheme: Newton is Chrysostom's clause with a biography: of the very tares it is likely that many may change and become wheat. Every premature uprooting forecloses an Amazing Grace. The No that spared him has not been retired — it is standing guard tonight over the stalks you have loved longest and hoped over least.

modules.heading: The Saboteur's Wager
modules.content: Count the enemy's appearances in the story: one. He comes while the household sleeps, sows, and slips away, and the plot never requires him again. That is the economy of skilled sabotage. Darnel was never going to strangle the wheat; the Master's own plan assumes both can stand in the same soil until harvest without the crop failing. The weeds' real leverage lay elsewhere: loyal hands, alarmed eyes, roots wound too deep for a clean pull. The enemy's single night reads like a wager on the servants' zeal: sow a weed, and hope to reap an uprooting. The Master's No is what losing that wager sounds like.
modules.historicalContext: The tactic was real enough for Roman law to remedy: the Digest preserves Ulpian, citing Celsus, granting a field's owner a lawsuit against anyone who maliciously sowed darnel or wild oats into his crop. Jesus' hearers did not have to imagine such an enemy — some of them had likely met one.

modules.heading: Three Sickles and a Bowed Head
modules.content:
The servants' offer survives in three domestic models. Check the shed.

The grief sickle. Somewhere in your life is a person you have stopped praying for — not out of malice but out of tiredness, because year after year the answer looked the same. The parable does not ask you to trust them again, excuse anything, or pretend the years away. It asks only this: stop finishing their story for them. Chrysostom's "room for change and improvement" is not a preacher's kindness; it is the Owner's standing policy, and Newton is that policy given four decades to work. So pray for that one today — once, specifically — as ground still in play. It will feel strange. Grief always resents being asked to hope again. Do it anyway.

The purity sickle. Some believers spend years shopping for a congregation with no darnel in it, leaving each church at the first flash of hypocrisy, certain the clean field is one move away. The parable retires the search: both grow together until the harvest is the condition of every field this side of the barn, which means a church with visible weeds is a church matching Jesus' description. Discernment survives — chapter 18 will teach private correction, and shepherds still guard flocks. But between correcting a brother and uprooting him lies a canyon, and the No governs its far side.

The roster sickle. Subtlest of all: the quiet sorting most of us run automatically — solid, suspect, solid, gone. Since wheat and darnel cannot be told apart until the heads form, every entry in that mental ledger is a guess wearing a robe. The stranger you wrote down as weeds may be wheat coming up through hard ground; the polished stalk you certified may be hollow. Catch yourself mid-sort once today and write the only thing the field permits this early: still growing.

And when the heads finally do form? The plate below shows how little interrogating the harvesters will need. A filled head of wheat grows heavy, and the weight bends its stalk toward the earth; darnel's head stays light, and its stalk stands stiff, straight, and tall to the very end. Fullness bows. Emptiness keeps perfect posture. That is the field's last word to its inspectors, too: in this story, the ones standing straightest — surest of their reading, quickest with a blade — are the servants. Fruit has weight, and weight bends the neck. If your certainty about someone else's soul never bends, check whether it is carrying anything.

Then hang the blade back on the wall and put the energy where it grows something: water, encourage, correct the way chapter 18 corrects. The sorting has a date and a crew, and the hiring was never yours to worry about.

modules.inlineImageAlt: Botanical plate: young wheat and darnel identical; at maturity wheat bows under a heavy golden head while darnel stands thin and erect
modules.inlineImageCaption: Young, wheat and darnel pass for one crop. At maturity the heads testify: wheat bows, heavy and gold; darnel stands stiff, straight, and empty. The inspection was always scheduled for harvest.

modules.passage: Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong. For they wither quickly like grass and wilt like tender plants. … Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him; do not fret when men prosper in their ways, when they carry out wicked schemes.
emphasis: Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him
modules.scriptureContext: David's answer to the servants' question, written a millennium before they raised it: the anxious eye sees grass that needs pulling today; the still heart knows grass withers on its own.

modules.prompt: Which sickle is actually yours — the grief that has stopped praying, the hunt for a cleaner field, or the roster you keep in your head — and what would hanging it up cost you this week?
additionalQuestions: Trace your fretting honestly: the replays, the refreshed feeds, the rehearsed indictments. What has any of it ever harvested?
The full head bends; the empty one stands straight. Where is your certainty about another person's soul standing straightest right now?
Someone once looked at the worst stretch of your life and chose patience over pulling. Who was it — and have you thanked God for what their waiting made room for?

modules.heading: Today's Practice: The Unfinished File
modules.instruction: A journaling exercise. Ten minutes, pen and paper — handwriting slows the verdicts down.

steps.title: Name the harvest you ran
steps.description: Write the name of the person you have most completely written off — for many of us, someone loved and far from God — and beneath it, the verdict you passed and roughly when you passed it.

steps.title: Reopen one file
steps.description: Under the verdict, copy Chrysostom's clause: 'it is possible for them even to become wheat.' Do not argue with it. Just let it sit under the name.

steps.title: Write the season you were given
steps.description: Now write two or three sentences about your own weediest stretch — and who, human or divine, declined to uproot you during it.

steps.title: Close with the verb
steps.description: End the page with one word, written large: aphete. Date it.

modules.heading: The Itch, Answered
modules.content:
The day opened in the dark: one enemy, one night, one bag of counterfeit seed. It closes with an inventory of what the light showed. An offer that sounded like loyalty and would have worked like sabotage. A No with three reasons — braided roots, eyes too early, and a mercy Jesus saves for tomorrow's telling. A psalmist who prescribed stillness for this exact fever a thousand years in advance. A slave-ship captain whom every fair reading condemned and every decade quietly disproved. And a botany lesson that doubles as a warning: fullness bows, and the stalk that stands straightest may be carrying the least.

None of it makes the Owner casual about darnel. The bundles and the burning are still in the parable, still ahead; the harvest is real, and it is dated. What the No refuses is not judgment but volunteers. Between now and then the field grows on under a patience that is neither blindness nor delay for its own sake — it is the same verb you pray whenever you ask forgiveness for yourself, extended over ground you would have cleared.

So end where the day began, with the name that surfaced while you read. Their stalk stands in an open field, under a No that has not expired, in a season no servant has authority to close. The enemy spent his one night; the Owner is spending every day since. You were not asked to referee that contest. You were asked to wait well: water what you can reach, and leave the blade where it hangs.

Tomorrow Jesus takes the disciples indoors and interprets the whole story Himself — the field, the enemy, the harvest, and reapers whose job description will surprise you. Tonight, David's word is enough to sleep on: be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him. The field has never once been unwatched.

modules.heading: Prayer
modules.prayerText: Patient Master, I confess how I have prayed: fretting dressed as intercession, inspection dressed as love. You watched Your field sabotaged and never raised Your voice; I meet rumors with a full campaign. Forgive the grip I keep on the blade — I am setting it down tonight. Thank You for everyone who ever looked at my half-grown life, saw what looked like weed, and stayed still. And for the name I have carried through this whole page: guard their ground, keep their growing, and make me rain and not a blade to them. Be still, You said through David. Make me still the way You are still — not absent, but watching, with the date already set. Aphete: let. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: Inhale: Let both grow — Exhale: until the harvest.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will pray once today — by name, specifically — for the person I had stopped praying for, refuse the first replay of the old evidence when it starts, and spend that energy watering something God is visibly growing.

receivingFromCross: The calm of an Owner who would not be baited into an early harvest

modules.heading: Community Reflection
modules.question: "Let both grow together" — the command ἄφετε (aphete) is built on the same Greek verb that Matthew's Gospel uses for what?
options: To forgive — as in 'forgive us our debts' (Matthew 6:12)
To judge at the proper time
modules.explanation: Aphete is the imperative of aphiēmi (G863) — release, leave, permit, and throughout Matthew, forgive. The Master's field policy and the disciple's daily pardon share one verb: the patience of the mixed field is forgiveness-shaped.

modules.heading: A Voice From the Story
modules.name: John Chrysostom
modules.bio: The 'golden-mouthed' preacher of the early church, whose verse-by-verse homilies through Matthew remain among the oldest complete expositions we possess. Made archbishop of Constantinople against his will, he preached against the excesses of court and clergy until the empire exiled him — twice. He died on the second forced march. A man who knew what it was to be treated as darnel by the field's self-appointed inspectors preached, in Homily 46, the parable's mercy with both edges intact.
modules.keyQuote: So long as they stand by the wheat, we must spare them, for it is possible for them even to become wheat.
modules.lessonForUs: Chrysostom heard in the Master's No both a shield for the saints and an open door for the tares — and the church that exiled him proved how badly every generation needs the reminder.

modules.heading: Sources & Related Study

relatedScriptures.text: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." — the same verb (aphiēmi) that lets both grow.
"Do not fret over those who do evil… Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him." — the psalmist's counsel for the servants' itch, ten centuries early.
"If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately..." — correction remains; uprooting is what's forbidden.

resources.title: John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Gospel of St. Matthew, Homily XLVI — NPNF First Series Vol. 10 (trans. Prevost, rev. Riddle)
resources.description: Source of both Chrysostom quotations, verbatim from the NPNF text: the danger of overthrowing saints with heretics, and the tares' possibility of becoming wheat. Free at ccel.org and newadvent.org.

resources.title: Augustine, Sermons on Selected Lessons of the New Testament, Sermon XXIII §§3-4 — NPNF First Series Vol. 6 (trans. MacMullen); and Letter 185 (On the Correction of the Donatists) §15
resources.description: Source of 'they who to-day are tares, may to-morrow be wheat' and the threshing-floor answer to the Donatist demand for a purified church before the final winnowing.

resources.title: John Newton — primary sources
resources.description: An Authentic Narrative (1764), Letters VIII, XIII-XIV — the storm of March 21, 1748 kept as a lifelong anniversary, the three post-conversion voyages as slave-ship captain with Sunday worship on deck, and the 1754 illness that ended them; Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade (1788) — his published confession, quoted verbatim. His later pastorate and hymnody are documented record. The six post-conversion trading years are kept in this telling because Newton's own texts insist on them.

resources.title: Greek data
resources.description: aphete / aphiēmi (G863, the Matthew 6:12 forgiveness verb), synauxanesthai (G4885, NT hapax) — BibleHub interlinear and Strong's, Matthew 13:30.

resources.title: Darnel — botanical and legal background
resources.description: Easton's Bible Dictionary, 'Tares': "It bears the closest resemblance to wheat till the ear appears, and only then the difference is discovered." Roman law treated malicious darnel-sowing as an actionable civil wrong: Digest 9.2.27.14 (Ulpian, citing Celsus) gave the field's owner a lawsuit against the saboteur.

modules.forDeeperStudy: Read Matthew 18:15-35 beside today's text — the private confrontation, the church's process, and the unforgiving servant — and watch Jesus hold correction and patience together without ever handing anyone the sickle.
